newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrians, angry over cuts, vote in Euro-poll.
newsitem.headline: Austrians, angry over cuts, vote in Euro-poll.

text.p: Austrians began voting on Sunday in a European parliamentary election in the first test of the government's popularity since it introduced an austerity budget cutting welfare benefits and raising taxes.

With European Union membership being blamed by many for the country's ills, the far-right Freedom Party which campaigned against the Maastricht treaty on EU integration was hoping to pick up protest votes to push its support towards its target 25 percent.

Pollsters said almost half the electorate was undecided and two-thirds of those were considering registering their anger at Chancellor Franz Vranitzky's government over tough economic belt-tightening.
Some 5.8 million voters are eligible to vote in the first Euro-poll held in Austria to fill the 21 seats allocated to the Alpine republic in the Strasbourg-based European Parliament.
Vienna state elections to determine the makeup of Austria's richest and most powerful province was also taking place.
Polling stations opened at 7 a.m. (0500 GMT) and will close at 6 p.m. (1600 GMT) when the first computer projections of the results were expected.
Sunny weather across Austria could push the turnout a touch higher than the 83 percent at the last general election in December when voters battled against snow storms to reach polling stations.
The Interior Ministry said security had been tightened following bomb threats from suspected rightwing extremists.
The Euro-election was the first nationwide vote since the general election and the introduction of a tough two-year budget in March which has hit the average Austrian hard.
Many Austrians have blamed membership of the European Union over the past 22 months for record bankrupties, a series of company takeovers by foreign firms and rising unemployment.

Far-right leader Joerg Haider has accused the ruling coalition of Social Democrats and conservative People's Party of bungling Austria's entry into the EU and has demanded the renegotiation of net annual payments to Brussels of around 15 billion schillings ($1.5 billion).
The Social Democrats saw its support dip in one opinion poll to 31 percent, the lowest level since World War Two, and down from 38 percent last December.
The People's Party has held steady at around 28 percent, helped by the personal appeal of its leading EU candidate Ursula Stenzel, an Austrian television personality.

Karl Habsburg, the grandson of last ruler of the Austro-Hungarian empire, is standing as number two on the People's Party list and is almost assured a seat in the European assembly. His father, Otto, is a German MEP.

The "feel-bad" factor could also have repercussions in the Vienna state election. Opinion polls have suggested Vranitzky's Social Democrats could lose their majority control of the capital for the first time since 1945.
The Social Democrats, who have used Vienna as its policy showcase for half a century, may be forced to rule the city in coalition with the conservatives or the leftist Green Party.
